TOPIC_REFERENCE: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) — Durability vs Write Latency
SECTION_TITLE: The Durability Dilemma: Mechanical Disks vs Volatile Memory
SECTION_BODY:
Every database starts with an uncompromising physical conflict: non-volatile storage is persistent but slow, while random access memory is fast but ephemeral. Before data models exist, physics dictates durability.

When an application issues a financial balance transfer, it cannot afford to acknowledge success until the transaction is durably committed. But physical storage devices operate under mechanical and electronic latency floors. When an operating system executes an fsync()💡 fsync()POSIX System CallA blocking kernel system call that forces the operating system to flush all modified in-memory data for a file descriptor down through hardware write buffers directly onto non-volatile storage media before returning control. syscall, execution pauses while the storage controller flushes Dirty Pages💡 Dirty PagesOS Memory ManagementPages of memory in the OS Page Cache that have been modified by an application process in RAM but have not yet been synchronized to non-volatile physical storage. to persistent platters or flash cells.

On a traditional rotational disk, a random write requires physically positioning an actuator arm over a magnetic track (seek time) and waiting for the platter to spin into place (rotational delay)—costing roughly 10 milliseconds (ms) per operation. Even on modern NVMe solid-state drives, random writes must navigate block erase cycles and flash translation layers, costing 20 to 100 microseconds.

⚡ The Core Architectural Dilemma

Consider the impossible trade-off faced by a database engine processing 10,000 transactions per second:

  • Naive Extreme 1: Direct Synchronous Random Writes: Every transaction directly modifies database table pages and calls fsync() to ensure safety.
    The Math / Physical Limit: At 10 ms per random disk seek, a single drive can process at most 1 ÷ 0.010 s = 100 writes/second. The database bottlenecks at 100 TPS while CPUs sit 99.9% idle.
  • Naive Extreme 2: Pure In-Memory Buffering: The database buffers all modifications in volatile DRAM with 0.01 ms latency, but a sudden crash permanently vaporizes uncommitted memory pages, corrupting financial balances.

How can a storage system achieve the durability of persistent storage without paying the crippling latency penalty of random disk writes on every client request? This fundamental friction led directly to the invention of the Write-Ahead Log (WAL).
